Asian Train Guide

Who runs the trains across Asia and what each one actually gets you — the Shinkansen and the Chinese G-trains, the overnight sleepers through Vietnam and Thailand, India's Rajdhani network, and the hill lines people ride for the ride. For each: where it is based, which countries it crosses, its key routes, and a straight read on what the journey is like. Eastern & Oriental Express
BELMOND · luxury sleeper
Scenic
Origin / Hub
🇸🇬 Singapore 🇲🇾 Malaysia
Countries Crossed & Served
🇹🇭 Thailand
↔
Key Routes
Singapore ↔ Kuala Lumpur (multi-night, seasonal)
Kuala Lumpur ↔ Bangkok (via Penang, Kanchanaburi)
Malaysian loop itineraries from Singapore (3–4 nights)
What it is like

This is a cruise that happens to run on rails, priced accordingly — think four figures a night, not a train fare. Cabins are teak-panelled and genuinely small; the observation car at the back is where the trip actually happens. Worth it if the journey is the holiday, absurd if you just want to reach Bangkok — the sleeper on the ordinary Thai network covers similar ground for a rounding error of the price.

KERETAPI TANAH MELAYU (KTMB)
Intercity

Johor Bahru ↔ Woodlands, Singapore (Shuttle Tebrau, 5 min)
Butterworth ↔ Padang Besar (Thai border connection)
What it is like

The ETS is the quiet success story of South-East Asian rail — electric, punctual, air-conditioned, and cheap enough that the parallel flight rarely makes sense once you count airport time. Book ahead: the Kuala Lumpur–Penang runs sell out days in advance around holidays. The five-minute Shuttle Tebrau into Singapore is the single best border crossing in the region and sells out a month out, which catches almost everyone.

🇯🇵 Japan
Shinkansen
JR GROUP · JR Central / East / West / Kyushu / Hokkaido
High-Speed
Origin / Hub
🇯🇵 Japan
↔
Key Routes
Tokyo ↔ Kyoto ↔ Osaka (Tokaido, Nozomi ~2h 15m to Kyoto)
Osaka ↔ Hiroshima ↔ Hakata/Fukuoka (Sanyo)
Tokyo ↔ Sendai ↔ Aomori (Tohoku, Hayabusa)
Tokyo ↔ Kanazawa ↔ Tsuruga (Hokuriku)
Aomori ↔ Hakodate ↔ Sapporo extension (Hokkaido, under construction)
What it is like

The benchmark every other railway is measured against, and it earns it: departures to the second, seats that recline without invading the row behind, and a cleaning crew that turns a train around in seven minutes. Reserve a seat if you have luggage — oversized bags now need a booked slot on Tokaido services, and unreserved cars fill first. Sit on the right leaving Tokyo for Fuji. The one catch is that the Japan Rail Pass is not valid on Nozomi, the fastest Tokaido service.

Japan Rail Pass
JR GROUP · national + regional passes
Rail Pass
Origin / Hub
🇯🇵 Japan
↔
Coverage
National pass: 7, 14 or 21 consecutive days, all JR lines
Regional: JR East, JR West Kansai, JR Kyushu, Hokkaido
Excludes Nozomi and Mizuho — the fastest Tokaido/Sanyo services
What it is like

The 2023 price rise changed the arithmetic and a lot of advice online has not caught up. A national pass now needs roughly a Tokyo–Kyoto–Hiroshima–Tokyo run before it beats buying tickets outright; a Tokyo–Kyoto return alone does not. Regional passes are where the value moved. Do the sum on your actual itinerary before buying — for most one-week trips built around two cities, individual tickets now win.

Sunrise Izumo & Sunrise Seto
JR WEST / JR SHIKOKU · Japan's last scheduled sleeper
Night Train
Origin / Hub
🇯🇵 Japan
↔
Key Routes
Tokyo ↔ Izumoshi (Izumo, ~12h)
Tokyo ↔ Takamatsu (Seto, ~10h) — the two split at Okayama
What it is like

The only regular overnight train left in Japan, and it books out the moment the window opens a month ahead — private cabins go in seconds. The Nobinobi Zaseki carpeted berth is included with a rail pass and is the cheapest bed in the country, though it is a flat mat, not a bunk. Ride it for the fact of it: watching the two halves separate at Okayama at dawn is the point, not the speed.

JAPAN'S PRIVATE RAILWAYS · limited express network
Private Operator
Origin / Hub
🇯🇵 Japan
↔
Key Routes
Tokyo (Shinjuku) ↔ Hakone (Odakyu Romancecar)
Tokyo (Asakusa) ↔ Nikko (Tobu Spacia)
Osaka / Kyoto ↔ Nara ↔ Ise (Kintetsu, incl. Shimakaze)
Osaka ↔ Kansai Airport (Nankai Rapi:t)
Osaka ↔ Kyoto ↔ Kobe (Hankyu)
What it is like

The private lines are where Japanese rail gets characterful — front-window observation seats on the Romancecar, the Shimakaze's lounge car, Nankai's Rapi:t looking like a submarine. They are also the reason a JR pass sometimes strands you: none of these are JR, so none are covered, and Hakone or Nikko will cost extra whatever pass you hold. Reservations are cheap and worth taking for the seat, not the speed.

CHINA RAILWAY · Fuxing & Hexie
High-Speed
Origin / Hub
🇨🇳 China
Countries Crossed & Served
🇭🇰 Hong Kong 🇱🇦 Laos
↔
Key Routes
Beijing ↔ Shanghai (~4h 20m, the flagship line)
Beijing ↔ Xi'an ↔ Chengdu ↔ Chongqing
Guangzhou ↔ Hong Kong West Kowloon (~48 min)
Shanghai ↔ Hangzhou ↔ Huangshan
Kunming ↔ Vientiane, Laos (China–Laos Railway)
What it is like

The largest high-speed network on earth and, on the trunk routes, the easiest way to move around China — second class is perfectly comfortable and first buys width rather than service. The trains are the simple part; the stations are not. Treat them like airports: security, ID checks and a twenty-minute walk to the platform, so arrive well before departure. Your passport is your ticket, and it is checked more than once.

Shanghai Maglev
SHANGHAI MAGLEV TRANSPORTATION · 430 km/h
High-Speed
Origin / Hub
🇨🇳 China
↔
Key Routes
Pudong Airport ↔ Longyang Road (7 min 20 s)
What it is like

The fastest commercial train in the world and a seven-minute novelty — it tops 430 km/h only on some departures, and 300 km/h on the rest, so check the board if the number is why you are there. It drops you at Longyang Road, which is not the city centre, so most people still need a metro leg afterwards. Ride it once for the speedometer; take the metro if you are simply trying to reach your hotel with luggage.

Qinghai–Tibet Railway
CHINA RAILWAY · highest railway in the world
Scenic
Origin / Hub
🇨🇳 China
↔
Key Routes
Xining ↔ Lhasa (~21h, Tanggula Pass 5,072 m)
Beijing / Shanghai / Chengdu ↔ Lhasa (40h+ through services)
What it is like

Genuinely extraordinary and genuinely demanding: the carriages are pressurised and pipe oxygen to every berth because the line crosses ground where the air is roughly half sea-level. Soft sleeper is the only class worth booking for a night at that altitude. The hard part is not the train — foreign visitors need a Tibet Travel Permit arranged through a tour operator before a ticket can be issued at all, so this is never a spontaneous trip.

KTX
KORAIL · national operator
High-Speed
Origin / Hub
🇰🇷 South Korea
↔
Key Routes
Seoul ↔ Busan (Gyeongbu, ~2h 15m)
Seoul ↔ Gwangju / Mokpo (Honam)
Seoul ↔ Gangneung (Gyeonggang, for the east coast)
What it is like

Seoul to Busan in about two and a quarter hours makes the domestic flight pointless, and the network is refreshingly simple to use — English-language booking works properly, and the app is one of the better ones in Asia. Nothing about it is showy; seats are narrower than the Shinkansen and the catering is a vending machine. It is transport that works, which on this route is all anyone needs.

Private Operator

🇰🇷 South Korea
↔
Key Routes
Suseo (south Seoul) ↔ Busan
Suseo ↔ Mokpo
What it is like

Same tracks and same speeds as KTX, slightly cheaper, and it leaves from Suseo rather than Seoul Station — which is the whole decision. If you are staying in Gangnam it saves a cross-city trek; if you are anywhere north of the river it adds one. Korail passes are not valid on it, and its seats do not appear in Korail's app, so travellers routinely miss a departure that would have suited them better.

Taiwan High Speed Rail
THSRC · Shinkansen-derived 700T
High-Speed
Origin / Hub
🇹🇼 Taiwan
↔
Key Routes
Taipei ↔ Kaohsiung/Zuoying (~1h 45m)
Taipei ↔ Taichung ↔ Tainan
What it is like

Japanese trains with Taiwanese manners — quiet, punctual, and the length of the island in under two hours. The catch is geography: several "city" stations sit well outside the city they name, and Taichung and Tainan both need a connecting local train, which surprises people who budgeted door to door. Foreign-passport discount passes are good value if you are making more than one long hop.

Alishan Forest Railway
TAIWAN FOREST RAILWAY · 762 mm narrow gauge
Scenic
Origin / Hub
🇹🇼 Taiwan
↔
Key Routes
Chiayi ↔ Alishan (reopened 2024 after 15 years)
Alishan ↔ Zhushan (sunrise service)
What it is like

A narrow-gauge logging line that climbs from sugarcane flats into cloud forest by switchback and spiral, and it only came back into through service in 2024 after a long closure. Slow — that is the product. The pre-dawn Zhushan sunrise train is the famous one and is a scrum; the ordinary daytime climb from Chiayi is the better ride and almost nobody books it.

Intercity

🇨🇳 China

Key Routes
Hong Kong West Kowloon ↔ Guangzhou (~48 min)
West Kowloon ↔ Shenzhen Futian (~14 min)
West Kowloon ↔ Beijing / Shanghai (long-distance sleepers)
What it is like

West Kowloon does mainland immigration inside the Hong Kong terminus, so the border is cleared before boarding and the train runs straight through — a genuinely clever piece of design that turns Shenzhen into a fourteen-minute hop. Budget the time you save into the terminus itself: check-in closes well before departure and the queues are real. Take your passport even for the short runs.

SRT · sleeper network from Bangkok
Night Train
Origin / Hub

Countries Crossed & Served

↔
Key Routes
Bangkok (Krung Thep Aphiwat) ↔ Chiang Mai (~13h overnight)
Bangkok ↔ Surat Thani (for Koh Samui / Phuket ferries)
Bangkok ↔ Hat Yai ↔ Padang Besar (Malaysian border)
Bangkok ↔ Nong Khai (for Vientiane, Laos)
What it is like

The newer Chinese-built sleeper carriages on the Chiang Mai run are a different world from the old stock — clean berths, curtains, working air-conditioning — and second-class air-con sleeper is the sweet spot; first buys a door, not a better night. Lower berths cost more and are worth it for the window. Long-distance services run late often enough that you should never book a same-morning connection off one.

VIETNAM RAILWAYS (ĐSVN)
Night Train
Origin / Hub
🇻🇳 Vietnam
↔
Key Routes
Hanoi ↔ Ho Chi Minh City (~33h end to end)
Hue ↔ Da Nang (the Hai Van Pass, ~3h)
Hanoi ↔ Lao Cai (for Sapa, overnight)
What it is like

Nobody should ride the full 33 hours unless they want to — the country's rail highlight is the three-hour Hue–Da Nang stretch over the Hai Van Pass, which is one of the great coastal rides anywhere and costs a few dollars in a soft seat. Sit on the sea side heading south. Four-berth soft sleeper is the sensible overnight class; the privately branded carriages attached to the Sapa trains are a real step up for a modest premium.

High-Speed

🇨🇳 China
↔
Key Routes
Vientiane ↔ Luang Prabang (~2h)
Vientiane ↔ Boten ↔ Kunming, China
What it is like

It turned a punishing ten-hour mountain road into a two-hour train, and that single fact has reshaped travel in Laos. Tickets are genuinely hard to get — they release a few days out and vanish, and foreigners generally do better through an agent or hotel than through the counter. Stations sit some way outside the towns they serve, so add a tuk-tuk at both ends before deciding it beats the bus.

Rajdhani, Shatabdi & Vande Bharat
INDIAN RAILWAYS · the premium network
Intercity
Origin / Hub
🇮🇳 India
↔
Key Routes
Delhi ↔ Mumbai (Rajdhani, overnight)
Delhi ↔ Agra ↔ Jhansi (Shatabdi / Vande Bharat, day)
Delhi ↔ Kolkata (Rajdhani, ~17h)
Mumbai ↔ Goa (Konkan Railway, monsoon-season scenery)
What it is like

Book early and book the right class and Indian Railways is superb value; do neither and it is a lesson. 2AC is the reliable choice for an overnight — curtained two-tier berths, bedding included — while 3AC is cheaper and markedly busier. Reservations open 60 days out and the popular Rajdhanis are gone the same morning. Foreign visitors should register on IRCTC before the trip, not at the station; the tourist quota exists but is not a substitute for planning.

Darjeeling Himalayan Railway
INDIAN RAILWAYS · UNESCO World Heritage, 2 ft gauge
Scenic
Origin / Hub
🇮🇳 India
↔
Key Routes
New Jalpaiguri ↔ Darjeeling (~7h, the full line)
Darjeeling ↔ Ghum (Joy Ride, ~2h, steam-hauled)
What it is like

The "toy train" is a two-foot-gauge line that loops and zigzags up to 2,200 m, often within touching distance of the road and the shopfronts beside it. The full run from the plains is a long, slow, frequently delayed day; most people are better served by the steam-hauled Ghum Joy Ride, which keeps the loops and the Batasia views and gives back five hours. Landslides close sections in monsoon — check before travelling.

Key Routes
Kandy ↔ Nanu Oya ↔ Ella (~7h through tea country)

What it is like

Deservedly famous, and now busy enough that the experience depends entirely on getting a reserved seat — book the observation or first-class carriage days ahead in season, or accept standing in a doorway for several hours, which is what the photographs actually show. The best scenery is Nanu Oya to Ella, so the shorter leg keeps the good part. Sit on the right leaving Kandy.

Haramain High Speed Railway
SAUDI ARABIA RAILWAYS (SAR) · 300 km/h
High-Speed
Origin / Hub
🇸🇦 Saudi Arabia
↔
Key Routes
Mecca ↔ Jeddah ↔ King Abdulaziz Airport ↔ Medina (~2h 20m)
What it is like

A Spanish-built 300 km/h line that replaced a punishing desert road drive between the two holy cities, and the airport stop makes it genuinely useful for arrivals into Jeddah. Modern, quiet, and heavily booked around Hajj and Ramadan, when capacity is the constraint rather than speed. Non-Muslim travellers cannot enter Mecca or Medina, which limits the line to the Jeddah legs.

YHT (Yüksek Hızlı Tren)
TCDD · Turkish State Railways
High-Speed
Origin / Hub
🇹🇷 Turkey
↔
Key Routes
Istanbul ↔ Ankara (~4h 30m)
Ankara ↔ Konya (~1h 45m)
Ankara ↔ Sivas (Eastern Express connection)
Doğu Ekspresi: Ankara ↔ Kars (~24h, winter scenic)
What it is like

The Istanbul–Ankara YHT is comfortable and cheap, though it leaves from Söğütlüçeşme or Pendik on the Asian side rather than the historic centre — factor in the cross-city leg. The famous train here is not the fast one: the Doğu Ekspresi to Kars is a 24-hour winter ride across the Anatolian plateau that sells out months ahead, and the tourist-branded version costs several times the ordinary fare for the same view.

What it is like

Spanish Talgo sets that make the Silk Road cities a comfortable day apart, and the single best way to travel Uzbekistan. Tickets go on sale a limited window ahead and the Tashkent–Samarkand runs sell out fast in spring and autumn, so book the moment the window opens. Stations have airport-style security and want your passport; leave more time than the short journey suggests.
